issues.legal_issue: A multi-storeyed residential building may be permitted on land after absolute title has passed to the purchaser when the final conveyance restricts the use of the property but does not prohibit such construction, and the applicable planning law imposes no building-height ceiling.
material_facts: The relevant purchasers had obtained absolute sale deeds before the disputed building permissions were granted.
The earlier lease-cum-sale terms restricted construction to one dwelling house while the allottee remained a lessee, but that restriction was not carried into the final conveyance.
The final conveyance required the building to be used for human habitation and prohibited specified non-residential uses; it did not prohibit a multi-storeyed building.
The Corporation granted permission for construction up to the third floor.
The Court found no relevant provision of the municipal or town-planning legislation imposing a ceiling on multi-storeyed construction.
issues.conclusion: The restriction to one dwelling house in the lease-cum-sale terms ceased to apply after absolute title was conveyed, and the municipal permission for construction up to the third floor did not violate the applicable Acts or Rules.
issues.legal_principle: Rules 17(4)–(7) of the City of Bangalore Improvement (Allotment of Sites) Rules, 1964, and Form II, particularly clauses 4 and 12–13, make the one-dwelling-house restriction applicable during the lease-cum-sale arrangement; on completion of that arrangement and transfer of absolute title, the final conveyance governs. Section 505 of the Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act, 1976, requires the Corporation to act consistently with the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961; section 14 of that Act requires development and land use to conform to the plan and regulations, but the Court found no applicable height ceiling. The Court held that Pee Kay Constructions v. Chandrashekar Hegde did not state good law on this point; the earlier Supreme Court disposition in that matter had not examined the High Court's reasoning on the merits.

rule.if: building_permission_case and absolute_title_transferred and final_conveyance_does_not_prohibit_multistorey_construction and planning_law_has_no_height_ceiling and municipal_permission_granted

predicates.building_permission_case: The proceeding concerns the legality of permission granted for construction of a building.
predicates.absolute_title_transferred: The original allottee or a successor obtained an absolute conveyance of the property before the disputed construction permission was granted.
predicates.final_conveyance_does_not_prohibit_multi: The final conveyance restricts the property's use but does not prohibit construction of a multi-storeyed building.
predicates.planning_law_has_no_height_ceiling: The applicable planning rules do not impose a ceiling on the number of floors or the height of the proposed building.
predicates.municipal_permission_granted: The municipal authority granted permission for the proposed construction.

issues.definition: When a building-permission proceeding concerns land whose absolute title has been transferred, the final conveyance does not prohibit multi-storeyed construction, the planning rules impose no height ceiling, and the municipal authority granted permission, the permission is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A public interest challenge to building construction may be denied when it is brought after substantial delay and construction has substantially progressed, particularly where interests of third parties have arisen.
material_facts: The construction began after permissions were granted and was stopped following an earlier High Court decision.
The Corporation later permitted construction to resume, and the public interest petition was filed after construction had resumed and was nearly complete.
Flat purchasers and occupants had acquired interests in the buildings before the petition was filed.
The Court found the delay fatal and held that third-party interests should not be disturbed in the circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The delay was fatal, and the public interest challenge did not justify disturbing the construction and interests that had arisen.
issues.legal_principle: Relief under Article 226 is discretionary, and delay and laches may make a petition unfit for relief even where a legal grievance is alleged. In State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhailal Bhai, the Court treated the limitation period for a comparable civil remedy as a guide to reasonable delay; Rabindra Nath Bose v. Union of India, Durga Prasad v. Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India, Ashok Kumar Mishra v. Collector, Raipur, and State of Maharashtra v. Digambar affirm that unexplained or blameworthy delay may justify refusal of discretionary relief, particularly where others have acted or acquired interests. The Court also reiterated from Balco Employees' Union v. Union of India and Dattaraj Nathuji Thaware v. State of Maharashtra that public interest litigation is an exceptional remedy to be used cautiously and by vigilant litigants for genuine public concerns.

rule.if: public_interest_challenge_case and challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay and construction_substantially_progressed and third_party_interests_arose

predicates.public_interest_challenge_case: A petitioner brought a proceeding in the public interest challenging the legality of a building or its construction.
predicates.challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay: The petitioner waited a substantial period after the challenged action before bringing the proceeding.
predicates.construction_substantially_progressed: The builder had substantially advanced or nearly completed construction before the challenge was brought.
predicates.third_party_interests_arose: People other than the builder acquired interests in or occupied the building before the challenge was brought.

issues.definition: When a public interest challenge is brought after substantial delay, construction has substantially progressed, and third parties have acquired interests, relief is denied for delay.
